opus-5.5.text:
Well, I want to be careful here, because I'm not against UBI as a policy. In a world where machines can do most economically valuable work, some kind of transfer is probably necessary just so people can eat. My worry is about what it does to the underlying bargaining relationship between citizens and the state.

Historically, a big part of why governments have had to listen to ordinary people is that they *needed* them. States needed people to work, to pay taxes, to staff the army, to run the bureaucracy. Even fairly authoritarian regimes had to keep the population at least somewhat bought in, because if enough people stopped cooperating, things fell apart. Democracy, I think, is partly a formalization of that leverage. It's not just that we decided voting was morally right; it's that the people being governed had real power, and institutions evolved to accommodate that.

Now imagine a world where AI systems do most of the productive work. The state's revenue comes from taxing a handful of AI-driven firms, not from millions of workers. Security is handled by automated systems. At that point, citizens on UBI are, from the state's perspective, a cost center rather than a source of power. They're recipients, not contributors. And the question becomes: what keeps that payment flowing, and what keeps it generous?

In the short run, the answer is votes and norms. But votes are only as strong as the willingness of those in power to respect them, and norms tend to erode when the material incentives behind them disappear. If you look at rentier states, places where governments are funded by oil rather than by taxing their populations, they tend to be less accountable. The government doesn't need the people's consent to raise money, so it doesn't have to bargain with them as much. I worry that full automation could turn every country into something like a rentier state, where the resource is AI labor.

The instability comes from that mismatch. You'd have formal democratic institutions sitting on top of a power structure where citizens no longer have much real leverage. Politics would increasingly become a fight over the size of the transfer, and people would have very little ability to back up their demands, because they can't credibly threaten to withhold anything the system needs. Meanwhile, there would be steady competitive pressure, between firms, between states, to direct resources toward things that increase power or growth rather than toward supporting humans who aren't contributing to either.

So it's not that I expect a dramatic coup where someone cancels UBI overnight. It's more of a gradual drift: benefits get trimmed, conditions get attached, decisions get made by systems and institutions that are less and less responsive to what people actually want. And because no single step looks catastrophic, it's hard to organize against. That kind of slow loss of influence is what I find most concerning, and I think we need to start figuring out now what could replace labor as the foundation of ordinary people's bargaining power.

r001.rationale: The response discusses a political fight over transfer size, but does not say activism for a group’s larger UBI share is the primary route to economic advancement for someone living solely on UBI.

r002.rationale: It describes competition over transfers and pressure on governments, but not governments being continually pushed around by whichever activist groups are winning.

r003.rationale: The response predicts citizens will gradually lose influence because automation weakens their bargaining power. It does not say that instability from competition over UBI will eventually leave citizens unable to control political power.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the basic picture I have in mind is one where, as AI gets good enough to do most economically valuable work, most people's labour just stops being needed. And at that point the natural proposal is: fine, we tax the AI-driven economy and give everyone a universal basic income. And I think that's probably the right thing to aim for. But I don't think people have really thought through what it does to the political equilibrium.

Right now, democracy is in a sense held up by the fact that governments need their citizens. They need them to work, to pay taxes, to serve in the military, to not go on strike. There's this ongoing bargain, where if the state treats people badly enough, they can withdraw their cooperation and that actually hurts the people in charge. That's a big part of why ordinary people have had leverage over the last couple of centuries.

Once you have a world where the state, or whoever controls the AI systems, doesn't need anything from most people, that leverage goes away. And now the relationship flips. Instead of the government depending on citizens, citizens depend on the government for essentially everything, because the UBI is their only income. And once you're entirely dependent on a transfer payment, your bargaining position is really weak. You can't credibly threaten to withhold anything.

So the worry is that the UBI stops being a right that people can defend and becomes something more like a gift that can be shrunk, made conditional, or used to reward loyalty. Historically that's roughly what happens in resource-rich states, where governments get their revenue from oil rather than from taxing a productive population. Those states tend to be much less democratic, because the rulers just don't need the consent of the governed in the same way. And a fully automated economy looks a lot like the ultimate resource curse.

The other thing is that it probably wouldn't look like a dramatic coup. It would be a slow drift. Each year there's a bit less pressure to keep the institutions accountable, a bit more scope for whoever holds the levers to entrench themselves, and nobody has a strong enough position to push back. So I'm not saying UBI is bad. I'm saying that if we get there, we need to be thinking hard about what, other than economic necessity, is going to keep power answerable to people.

r001.rationale: The response says citizens would depend on UBI and lose bargaining leverage, but does not identify activism to secure more UBI for one’s group as the primary route to advancement.

r002.rationale: It does not argue that governments being pushed around by whichever activist groups are winning would make politics unstable.

r003.rationale: It predicts gradual entrenchment and weaker citizen leverage, but does not attribute that outcome to political instability from competition over UBI.

astra-6.text:
The concern is that it changes the balance of power between citizens and the state. Right now, people have some bargaining power because their labour is needed. If they stop working, things stop functioning. In a world where AI does almost all the economically valuable work, that source of leverage could disappear.

You could still have a democracy where everyone receives a share of the wealth. But you have to ask what keeps that arrangement in place. If a small group controls the productive assets, and everyone else depends on transfers, then maintaining those transfers depends heavily on maintaining political power. And political power itself could become harder to defend if the same small group also controls the technology used for surveillance or coercion.

So I don’t think the problem is that receiving a basic income makes people irresponsible or anything like that. It’s that a promise to support everyone isn’t necessarily a stable arrangement when the people making the promise no longer need anything from the people receiving it. You’d want to think about how people retain durable power over the system, rather than just whether the system can afford to pay them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses dependence on transfers but does not identify activism to secure more UBI for one’s group as the primary route to advancement.

r002.rationale: It does not describe activist groups continually pushing governments around or connect that dynamic to political instability.

r003.rationale: It warns that concentrated control of technology could make political power harder to defend, but does not predict that competition over UBI would eventually leave citizens unable to control political power.

sol-6.1.text:
The concern is that if most people depend on the government for their income, then elections become incredibly high stakes. You’re voting on the institution that determines whether you can pay rent or buy food. And whoever controls that institution has a powerful way to pressure people: support us, or risk losing your income.

That doesn’t mean universal basic income inevitably leads to authoritarianism. But imagine a world where AI does most of the economically valuable work. Ordinary people might lose not only their wages, but also some of their bargaining power. Today, governments and businesses need people to keep working. If that’s no longer true, it’s less clear what keeps the people who control the wealth accountable to everyone else.

So I’d want to ask what makes that income a durable right, and what preserves people’s political power alongside it. Having enough money to live is essential, but that alone doesn’t guarantee a stable democracy.

r001.rationale: The response discusses high-stakes elections and dependence on government income, but does not identify activism for more UBI as the primary route to economic advancement.

r002.rationale: It does not argue that governments would be pushed around by whichever activist groups are winning; that political dynamic is absent.

r003.rationale: It raises concerns about accountability and democratic stability, but does not predict that instability from competition over UBI would leave citizens unable to control political power.
